posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
In connection with Blyth Colour Tuning of DCG, I was wondering how the dryness of a DCG layer might be measured. The only related device that comes to mind is the "moisture meter" for wood. These are based on the electrical resistance of wood, moist wood having lesser resistance.

It might be possible to take a voltmeter, switch it to resistance mode (ohms), and put the probe tips (close together) into contact with the gelatin layer. When I have the chance, I will give this a try. I think really dry layers of gelatin will need to be tested (to determine what is "adequate" for sealing), so the high resistance ranges may be involved, probably coupled with high resolution or sensitivity.

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
I did some quick testing of the electrical resistance of a DCG layer, and it turns out it's very high, and maybe this is partially due to the thinness of the layer (which is around 10 microns). I took an old MBDCG hologram (Jeff's formula) which had been exposed to ambient conditions (stored in an unheated shed) and tried to measure the resistance. This layer was way too damp for sealing, as the shed is quite humid. Anyway, the resistance was off the scale (I'm not sure how many megaohms my digital meter can register though). Then I wet the DCG layer under the faucet, wiped it off, and tried again. This time the resistance was around 20 megaohms, with the probes as close together as I could get (without having them touch each other).

I tried some wood as well (a piece of oak that I had in the basement, which is damp). This did not register either. Then I wet the wood, and was able to get resistances in the 10 to 20 megaohm range, even if the probe tips were held very far apart, which surprised me.

What this tells me is that a commerical wood moisture meter must be much more sensitive than a simple ohm-meter. So there must be different electronics to measure very high resistances (because the piece of oak should have easily registered, before wetting, on a commercial moisture meter).

So maybe the idea has promise, if an ohm-meter can be built that registers ultra-high resistances.

posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** OK, I found out these meters do exist, they are called "megohm meters" and are used to test insulation. For example:http://www.testequipmentdepot.com/fluke ... s/1503.htmBut at $319 it's still pricey (for an experiment). If someone has one already, however, it would be interesting to see if the dryness of gelatin can be determined with it. I feel optimistic that it can, since it can measure resistances between 0.1 megohm and 2000 megohms.

The way thin materials have their resistances measured is in “ohms per square”, because it is independent of the size of the square . But for that to be so the opposite sides of a square have to be relatively perfect conductors. I used to do this with the (generally available) “silver conductive paint” painted along 2 opposite edges . 

(However I would not buy “epoxy” based silver conductive paints which would probably be quite unsuitable as temporary electrical contacts).

Although the paint is supposed to be baked after application to bring its resistance down to negligibly low level, when you are dealing with the high resistance levels you have found then it is enough to just let the paint dry without baking and then after you have made your ohmeter measurement it can be completely wiped off the gelatin film with an acetone soaked tissue. So to get an “ohms per square” reading on say a 5” x 4” hologram , you need to put one strip of paint along the 4 inch side and then a second parallel stripe 4 inches away, being acetone based it will not scar a DCG 

hologram. You should get exactly the same resistance reading as the same gelatin hologram in a 2” x 2” or 8 x 8” format. 

Jeff

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: Tom B.
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
Since both gelatin and pure water are essentially non-conductive, resistance measurements will be strongly dependant on the degree of ionic contamination (by salts etc.) of the water/gelatin mixture. I expect it will be difficult to translate resistance measurements into moisture content without some other independent means of measuring moisture and gelatin thickness to calibrate the measurements for a given batch of emulsion. 

It should be possible to measure moisture content by weighing the plate on a sensitive scale before and after baking in a dry environment. A 100 mm^2 plate with 10 micron emulsion, would, if the emulsion was 100% water (obviously impossible), show a change of (100 mm^2 * .01 mm) = 100 mm^3 or 0.1 cc (0.1 gram) after baking (if my math is right), so the change should be large enough to be measurable with a scale that can resolve milligrams.

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: Hans
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
I think you made a mistake with your math Tom,

If we have a plate with size 100mm^2 = 10mmx10mm.

And the layer is 10um = 0.01mm thick.

The volume of the gelatin would be: 10x10x0.01mm^3 = 1mm^3.

One cc is 10x10x10mm. So the volume of your gelatin would be 0.001cc. With a weight of 1 microgram if it had fully absorbed the water.

If have a lab scale that has a resolution of 0.05g, but it can weigh a maximum of 150g. So, in my case increasing the plate size would create a problem with the maximum weight that can be measured.

Perhaps it would be sufficient to just use a sheet of gelatin and first dry it without submersion in the citric acid. Weigh it. And then take that same sheet and sub it in citric acid, dry it, and weigh it again. The difference would indicate the amount of water retained due to the citric acid.

But I still don't understand why the residual water is so important with DCG. If the plate shows a hologram after drying and is then sealed, how will the state of the hologram alter after sealing? Why not just seal it and mis-treat it with repeated heat and cold exposure and see what happens? If it works, it works.

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** But I still don't understand why the residual water is so important with DCG. If the plate shows a hologram after drying and is then sealed, how will the state of the hologram alter after sealing?

According to Rallison:

"Baking at about 150 C will cause the gelatin to densify and if tilted fringes are present they will appear to lay down, baking also makes the gel much more stable and a little less hygroscopic. While it is still hot a glass cap or at least an epoxy coating can be applied without trapping too much moisture in the film. Trapped moisture can become active upon heating and cause the gel to collapse here and there and everywhere. Mysterious color shifts in capped reflection holograms can be explained by the action of trapped moisture and lack of 150 bake down."

I was searching for another comment by Rallison, and although I couldn't find it, it was something to the effect that "all" of the DCG holograms he ever did that did **not**receive the final baking failed eventually.

So this is why I'm harping on the subject. I guess you could say my "dream" for a long time has been to find a DCG tuning method that can be done in the dry state (no noisy or damaging reprocessing) that does not depend on how much the layer has been dehydrated. There needs to be a certain level of dehydration for a DCG hologram, period. But if you are relying on dehydration (and here I mean by heating, which is the method used in the past) to color-tune, then you are manipulating a parameter which really shouldn't be manipulated. So basically what I mean is that, in this case (controlled shrinkage by baking), color-tuning and dehydation do not agree with each other, yet they are linked inseparably.

This is why Jeff's method is exciting to me. Dehydation is done solely for the purpose of dehydration, nothing else. Once that has been done adequately, then a completely different process can be used to tune the color (heating to cause controlled shrinkage). So there will be no compromise regarding dehydration.

Of couse, we don't know if this process will work out. Hopefully it will. One question on my mind is: why did Jeff's first hologram shrink upon baking, while the second hologram did not shrink upon dehydration? Assuming a process can be worked out, then it occurs to me that the initial dehydation should be measurable, at least at first, so that a protocol can be established.

Rallison and others indicate that a final bakeout is necessay, but dehydation without heat is slower and is not an established (documented) procedure in this application. So what I'm trying to do is measure the "equivalent dryness" for a dehydrated hologram, as compared to one that has received a standard bakeout. Jeff, will you please consider the following question: How does the dryness of a baked DCG hologram compare to one that has been dehydrated for a week?

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: dcgman
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
one way to measure the humidity content of the coating might be to expose a small area (say 1cm diameter) of the plate to a precise amount of microwave radiation. The change in temperature of the gel in the irradiated area would be an indication of the amount of moisture in the gel. You would need a sensitive infrared thermometer to do this.

Another possibility would be to have a microwave detector placed directly opposite the emitter. Interposing a gel coated plate between the two and measuring the resulting attenuation might provide the moisture content of the plate.

This technique need not be limited to microwaves- it could be done using Infra Red wavelengths which are strongly absorbed by water.

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?
posts.content_md:
Yes, in the reading research I have done, it has been stated that if you dry the gelatin to a 2% water content, the gelatin becomes insoluble to water again, just as the collagen was in which the gelatin was made. This is due to the extensive crosslinking achieved by dehydration. 

So , in using a scale:

Mix up 

1 gram of gelating

30 ml of water

.3 grams of sensitizer

Coat a large plate with entire amount

expose and process

Starting weight (we can elliminate the sensitizer as it is removed during processing) = 31 grams

Dry this to... (2% of 30 = .6 grams water) + (1 gram gelatin) = 1.6 grams.

At 1.6 grams the gelatin should be insoluble to water. 

Something I just thought of..... to be fully accurate here....

How much water is in the gelatin grains we are using? Obviously it cannot be 2% or less or the grains would not be soluble. I would assume the manufacturers of gelatin would not dry the gelatin too much as then it would be pretty useless. But no matter what they dry it to above the 2% I would assume the gelatin, being hydroscopic in its manufactured state, would equalize its water content with the ambient humidity it is exposed to. This needs to be considered or it will throw off you weight measurements. 

So how much water does 1 gram of off the shelf gelatin contain at 50% relative humidity? 20%? 70%......

posts.topic_title: resistance measurements of a gelatin layer?

posts.content_md:
That sounds like a simple and direct way of measuring moisture content, John.

This is an area of research that needs to be explored, that is, the dehydration of DCG. And specifically, the effects of drying DCG to different levels. I guess there are two scenarios, the longevity of sealed DCG holograms, and unsealed ones. Although I only think in terms of sealed DCG, the behavior of unsealed ones is interesting also.

Jeff Blyth said that leaving the DCG in a good desiccator for two weeks (no heat was involved) made his holograms impervious to water vapor damage (but not to contact with liquid water).

That's a good question about the water content of gelatin powder, I don't know what it might be. But you could use your same technique to measure that, I guess. Weigh it before and after dehydration. But you may need a vacuum oven for this purpose, because it seems that a standard desiccator like I made can only go down to about 14% RH. I don't know how this would change if it was done under a vacuum (no heat). But a vacuum oven seems like the ultimate way to go.

By the way John, do you have reference concerning that 2% figure, and for the idea that dehydration causes crosslinking?

Hey Joe....

I have holograms that I just boxed up that have been in my lab for years. They are not sealed and have not degraded at all. As I didn't use the lab that ofted I am sure it has undergone temperature swings from 40F to 100F and humidity levels at the 100F of up to 70% or more. I dried them hot and heavy with a hair dryer and usually overdo it by keeping up the drying process well after it seems the hologram has been completely dried. So I imagine the oven statement Jeff mention is 100% accurate.

Sure, the reference is footnoted on the wiki entry I wrote.

Here is the Wiki entry

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... CG_Process](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/The_Mechanics_of_Gelatin_and_the_DCG_Process)

And the source from Stanford University;

[http://albumen.stanford.edu/library/c20/kozlov1983.html](http://albumen.stanford.edu/library/c20/kozlov1983.html)

(about 1/3 the way down).

> A number of authors have thus considered water a necessary element for the formation of the collagen and gelatin helical structures. A definite amount of water is believed to be necessary to maintain the native conformation of collagen molecules4,6,96,99-106,111. The specific role of water in the formation of the helical structure has also been demonstrated for synthetic polypeptides isomorphous to collagen112 The effect of water on the mechanical properties of collagen and gelatin also provides some information, though indirectly, on the role of water in the formation of the collagen and gelatin helical structures. Gelatin dehydrated below a 2% moisture level becomes insoluble in water because of crosslinking between the gelatin macromolecules113. Dehydrated gelatin is thus a crosslinked polymer which makes it extremely brittle and hence unusable in the solid state. At 25±3% moisture content, gelatin undergoes transformation from the glassy to the rubbery state at room temperature114 The behaviour of gelatin in the two states above and below Tc manifests itself most clearly when gelatin is subjected to impact74. Figure 3 shows the dependence of resistance to impact of cold gelatin films on the relative pressure of water vapour (curve 1). The isotherm of sorption of water vapour by helical gelatin is also shown (curve 2). As can be seen from Figure 3, both curves can be subdivided into three regions. In the first region extending up to 0.12-0.13g/g moisture content (region 'a') the resistance to impact of gelatin increases gradually (up to P/P0~0.4) with moisture content. A comparison of this finding with the data in Table 4 shows that the increase results from the uptake of structural water.
